title: Lesson 35: Domain Modeling: Entities, Aggregates, and Bounded Contexts Applied to Agent Design
description: The domain modeling discipline of entities, aggregates, bounded contexts, and ubiquitous language, and how it keeps a multi-agent system from collapsing into a tangle of overlapping prompts.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Domain Modeling: Entities, Aggregates, and Bounded Contexts Applied to Agent Design”, a team is about to draw an agent graph for a claims intake system. What does the lesson say to draw first, and why?
options: The agent graph, because the tools actually available determine which responsibilities can be assigned.
A single agent covering triage, coverage, and adjudication, which the team splits later only if performance suffers.
The context map, because a bounded context is a conceptual boundary around a model while an agent is an implementation detail, and one context may use several agents.
The prompt library, because the vocabulary inside each prompt is what defines the boundaries.
questions.explanation: Do not equate agents with bounded contexts: the context map comes first, or the agent graph reproduces whatever tools happened to be available instead of the shape of the business.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The rule that an incident on a lapsed policy is not covered should live in the coverage agent’s prompt, because a model can reason about policy language.
The rule requires policy status, coverage dates, and the incident date to be read together, so it belongs in the aggregate with the policy as root and is checked only through the root.
The rule should be split across the triage and coverage tools so each one enforces the part it can see.
The rule should be enforced by the output schema, which is what typed contracts exist for.
questions.explanation: An aggregate is a consistency boundary, so anything that must stay true together is decided in one place behind the aggregate root rather than combined in free text by the agent.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Treating model output as a proposal requires the model to be deterministic before the domain can authorize a change.
A bounded context and an agent are the same thing, so one agent should cover every context it participates in.
Model output is an untrusted proposal: constrain and parse it, normalize against trusted context, authorize deterministically, then execute through the aggregate that enforces the invariant.
Synonyms for one concept should be preserved per prompt so each agent can use the vocabulary its audience prefers.
questions.explanation: A schema can reject a missing field but cannot decide whether the user owns the claim or whether a date resolves correctly, so authority for the state change sits in deterministic domain code.
